title: Pendulum

source.credit: Rendered by Ansatz with exactly known physics (L = 0.80 m, released at 70°)

slow_motion.evidence: No narration, captions, or on-screen text indicate slow motion; motion appears as continuous animation.

subjects.description: small blue spherical bob hanging from a thin string pivoted at the dark bar

observation.what_happens: A blue ball suspended by a string swings back and forth beneath a fixed pivot. It starts held high on the right and then oscillates continuously from side to side through the bottom for the whole clip.

calibration.note: no ruler needed: the swing is measured as an angle

given: g = 9.807 m/s² (Earth): hold g fixed and measure the pendulum's length L in metres from its swing
reasoning: Path is circular with 137 deg arc and theta +-1.2 rad so large-angle sin nonlinearity matters and small-angle law is a useful null. Peaks fall from 1.21 to 1.07 rad over ~4.5 s with period ~1.9 s, showing weak dissipation in air, so undamped vs linear-viscous vs quadratic-aerodynamic damping are genuinely different predictions for the held-back frames.

critique.finding: The ball swings like a long pendulum with length {L} and loses a tiny bit of swing each time from friction {b}.
critique.headline: String swing slows gently from slight friction.
critique.why_it_won: It captures the gentle even fading of the swing while quadratic air drag fades it unevenly.

headline: String swing slows gently from slight friction.
finding: The ball swings like a long pendulum with length 0.8 ± 0.0021 m and loses a tiny bit of swing each time from friction 0.0601 ± 0.00017 1/s.

eyeball.confidence: low - rough visual estimate from grid/scale and few swings, timing inferred
eyeball.law_in_words: Small-angle pendulum period T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) so L = g*(T/2*pi)^2 with g=9.81 m/s2, T estimated from zero-crossings/swing time in clip and cross-checked with grid length vs 1-m scale bar; amplitude envelope ~ exp(-b*t) for linear viscous damping, b estimated from slow decay of peak horizontal displacement over observed periods.
